Introduction:
Although the prevalence of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) varies across populations [ 1 ] and diagnostic methods [ 2 , 3 ], it has markedly risen over recent decades [ 4–6 ], with a pooled prevalence of 32.4% [95% confidence interval (CI): 29.9–34.9] and incidence of 46.9 cases per 1000 person-years in adults [ 3 ]. Men are more susceptible to developing NAFLD than women (70.8 vs. 29.6 cases per 1000 person-years) [ 3 ].

NAFLD, associated with a sedentary lifestyle, low physical activity, excessive calorie intake, and unhealthy diet [ 7 ], is considered a hepatic manifestation of metabolic syndrome [ 8 , 9 ] and a leading cause of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [ 10 ]. In South Korea, a study reported NAFLD prevalence of 33.6% among 25 947 participants, by using abdominal ultrasonography data, over a median follow-up of 7.5 years [ 11 ]. The HCC incidence was 23.1 vs. 0.9 per 100 000 person-years for those with and without NAFLD, respectively [ 11 ]. After adjusting for age, sex, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, gamma-glutamyl transferase, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) level, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) level, and triglyceride level, the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for NAFLD-associated HCC was 16.73 (95% CI: 2.09–133.85) [ 11 ]. Similarly, a study found an association between nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and HCC (HR: 3.49; 95% CI: 1.23–9.86) in a Japanese cohort with biopsy-confirmed NAFLD [ 12 ]. Recently, NAFLD was also linked to gastrointestinal cancer [ 9 ], cardiovascular diseases [ 1 ], and disability [ 6 ].

Given the lack of approved drugs for NAFLD treatment [ 13 ], researchers are exploring preventive strategies, focusing on personal traits such as phenotype [ 14 ] and lifestyle [ 13 ], and environmental exposures such as air pollutants and endocrine-disrupting chemicals [ 15 ]. According to the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021, high systolic blood pressure, smoking, and ambient fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) pollution were the top three risk factors for age-standardized attributable disability-adjusted life years in East Asia [ 16 ], including Taiwan. These findings emphasize the importance of raising awareness and the critical need to mitigate exposure to ambient PM 2.5 pollution and other risks.

Air pollutants, particularly PM 2.5 and traffic-related pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) and carbon monoxide (CO), pose significant health risks. PM 2.5 —fine particulate matter that is ≤2.5 μm in diameter—infiltrates alveoli and enters the bloodstream [ 17 , 18 ], increasing morbidity and mortality in respiratory infections, cardiovascular diseases, and type 2 diabetes [ 19 ]. Motor vehicle combustion is the primary source of ambient NO 2 [ 20 ] and CO [ 21 ]—both traffic-related air pollutants. NO 2 exposure is linked to pediatric asthma [ 22 ] and respiratory mortality [ 23 ], while short-term CO exposure is associated with increased hospital visits for myocardial infarction [ 24 ] and higher cardiovascular and respiratory diseases mortality [ 25 ].

Recent studies exploring associations between NAFLD and air pollution, particularly PM 2.5 , have yielded inconsistent results [ 26–28 ]. Some longitudinal studies reported positive associations between PM 2.5 exposure and NAFLD incidence [ 29 , 30 ] or fatty liver index [ 31 ]. Others identified proximity to major roadways [ 28 ] and NO 2 exposure [ 30 ] as NAFLD risk factors. Differences in study designs, exposure levels, PM 2.5 components [ 32 ], and NAFLD definitions may account for these discrepancies.

In Taiwan, efforts to mitigate air pollution have lowered PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO levels over recent decades [ 33 , 34 ]. Despite these improvements, epidemiological studies investigating associations between traffic-related air pollutants and NAFLD incidence remain limited. Using a time-dependent Cox proportional-hazards model, this study investigates the association of NAFLD incidence with PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO exposure.
Methods:
### Participants

Participants were selected from the MJ Health Research Foundation database, which collects health examination data and lifestyle information through questionnaires. The dataset included health records from company-provided and voluntary examinations for individuals and families [ 35 ]. From 135 399 screened participants, inclusion criteria were: health examinations conducted between 1996 and 2016; age of ≥20 years at enrollment; no history of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, or thyroid disease; [ 5 ] no history of gastrointestinal surgery; absence of NAFLD or liver cirrhosis on baseline ultrasonography; no reported alcohol consumption or hepatitis; and availability of at least two health examination records. Participants were required to have a registered address in Taiwan, excluding eastern regions (∼0.6% of the cohort) due to sparse air quality monitoring stations [ 33 ]. Individuals who relocated during follow-up were excluded due to challenges in assessing accurate cumulative exposure. Additional exclusions were participants with incomplete covariate data. Finally, 62 660 participants were included. Supplementary Figure S1 presents the selection process flowchart.

### NAFLD definition

Fatty liver disease and cirrhosis were diagnosed through abdominal ultrasonography by experienced physicians at the MJ Health Screening Center [ 36 ]. NAFLD was defined as “fatty liver” or “fatty liver with focal sparing,” excluding liver cirrhosis cases.

### Exposure evaluation

Daily PM 2.5 and NO 2 levels were estimated by using a hybrid Kriging land-use regression (LUR) model involving an extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithm [ 37 , 38 ] and CO levels were estimated by using LUR-XGBoost [ 39 ]. Models utilized daily air pollutant data from 68 fixed-site monitoring stations in western Taiwan. Meteorological variables, greenness, culture-specific emissions (e.g. temples, Chinese restaurants), proximity to the nearest power plant, garbage incinerators, and industrial parks were predictors for PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO [ 37–39 ]. Additionally, levels of co-pollutants such as SO 2 and O 3 were determined [ 37–39 ]. Daily ambient PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO levels were estimated with the aforementioned models and mapped at 50 m × 50 m resolution in ArcGIS. Personal exposure levels were based on residential township. Model performance (10-fold cross-validation) showed R 2 values of 0.93, 0.90, and 0.84, with root mean square error (RMSE) values of 4.73, 2.04, and 0.15 for PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO, respectively [ 37–39 ]. The exposure window was defined as the 3-year average before each health examination during follow-up.

### Covariates

Demographic data [ 3 , 5 , 28 , 30 ] were obtained through self-administered questionnaires, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), marital status (single/divorced/separated/widowed or married/cohabitating), educational level (junior high school or lower, senior or vocational high school, college degree, or master’s degree or higher), annual household income (<13 333, 13 333–40 000, or >40 000 USD) [ 40 ], smoking status (never, secondhand/former, or frequent smoker/daily smoker), sleep duration (<6, 6–8, or >8 hours/day), regular exercise (never/little, sometimes/1–4 h/week, or frequently/daily/>4 h/week), and fried-food consumption (none/little/≤1 portion, 2–3 portions, or ≥4 portions/week).

Given that NAFLD typically coexists with metabolic disorders [ 10 , 11 , 41 ], metabolic indicators, including abdominal obesity, hypertension, elevated fasting glucose, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL-C, and high LDL-C, were adjusted for. Waist circumference and blood pressure were nurse-measured, while biochemical data (triglycerides, HDL-C, LDL-C, fasting glucose) were analysed by using a Toshiba C8000 analyser [ 36 ]. Metabolic indicators were defined by using established criteria [ 42 ]. Abdominal obesity: waist circumference of ≥90 cm (Asian men) or ≥80 cm (Asian women). Hypertension: systolic blood pressure ≥130 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure ≥85 mmHg, or use of antihypertensives. Elevated fasting glucose: ≥100 mg/dL or hyperglycemic medication use. Hypertriglyceridemia: triglyceride level ≥150 mg/dL or medication use. Low HDL-C: <40 mg/dL (men) or <50 mg/dL (women) or medication use. High LDL-C: <130 mg/dL. Initial metabolic status was used in the analysis, as air pollution exposure may influence these indicators [ 43 ].

### Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics characterized participants and air pollutant levels. Spearman’s correlation established a matrix for all pollutants. For participants developing NAFLD, event time was the first NAFLD record; for others, the last examination before loss to follow-up or 31 December 2016 was right-censored.

Time-dependent Cox proportional-hazards models were used to calculate HRs and 95% CIs for NAFLD incidence. Covariates significant in univariate analysis were included in multivariate models. Two-pollutant models assessed changes after adjusting for another pollutant. Adjusted HRs per interquartile range (IQR) increase in PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO were computed. Sensitivity analyses were stratified by sex and modifiable behaviors (smoking, sleep duration, exercise, and fried-food consumption). Robustness was further validated by using augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW), combining inverse probability of censoring weighting with multiple imputations for a high censoring rate [ 44 ]. Model fit was assessed via Akaike and Bayesian information criteria (AIC, BIC). All analyses were performed by using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA).

Taiwan spans ∼36 000 km 2 , with a population of 21.5–23.5 million during 1996–2016 [ 45 ]. Participants were recruited from townships averaging 53.3 km 2 (range: 0.9–247.3 km 2 ). Supplementary Figure S2 shows Taiwan’s population density and the cohort distribution.
Results:
Between 1996 and 2016, 18 959 incident NAFLD cases were identified over 357 392 person-years (incidence: 53.0 per 1000 person-years).

### Distribution of ambient air pollutants

Table 1 shows the levels of PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO along with Spearman’s correlation coefficients. The median (IQR) values corresponding to the 3-year average levels of PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO were 30.7 (7.4) μg/m 3 , 22.0 (8.5) ppb, and 0.56 (0.27) ppm, respectively. Weak correlations existed between PM 2.5 and NO 2 ( r =
 0.26) and between PM 2.5 and CO ( r =
 0.30), while a strong correlation was noted between NO 2 and CO ( r =
 0.86). Supplementary Figure S3 depicts the geographical distributions of 3-year average of air pollutants and the proportion of new NAFLD cases. PM 2.5 levels increased from northern to southern Taiwan, while NO 2 and CO levels were higher in densely populated areas ( Supplementary Figure S2A ).

### Associations between individual characteristics and NAFLD incidence

Table 2 presents crude HRs showing associations between individual characteristics and NAFLD incidence. Baseline demographics are shown in Supplementary Table S1 . Participants developing NAFLD were predominantly ≥45 years old, men, with BMI of ≥24 kg/m 2 , married/cohabitating, or had unhealthy behaviors. Secondhand/former smokers, frequent smokers, sleep duration <6 h/day, exercise ≤4 h/week, higher fried-food consumption (≥2 portions/week), and those with any metabolic indicator assessed in this study showed increased NAFLD risk.

### Associations between exposure to ambient air pollutants and the incidence of NAFLD

Single-pollutant models adjusted for age, sex, and BMI ( Table 3 , Model 1) showed significant associations between 3-year average PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO exposure, and NAFLD incidence. Further adjustments for marital status, education, smoking, sleep, exercise, fried-food consumption ( Table 3 , Model 2), and initial status of metabolic indicators ( Table 3 , Model 3) yielded adjusted HRs that were consistent with those of Model 1. Model 3 demonstrated the best fit based on lower AIC and BIC values. Adjusted HRs were 1.04 (95% CI: 1.02–1.05) per 7.4-μg/m 3 PM 2.5 increase, 1.06 (95% CI: 1.04–1.09) per 8.5-ppb NO 2 increase, and 1.16 (95% CI: 1.13–1.19) per 0.27-ppm CO increase. Two-pollutant models confirmed the significance of each pollutant when adjusted for another. Exposure–response curves are shown in Supplementary Figure S4 .

Table 4 presents adjusted HRs using median 3-year pollutant levels as cut-offs: ≤30.2 μg/m³ for PM 2.5 , ≤21.6 ppb for NO 2 , and ≤0.56 ppm for CO. Compared with participants residing in areas with low levels of both PM 2.5 and NO 2 , those in areas with high levels of both pollutants had an adjusted HR of 1.25 (95% CI: 1.19–1.31). Similarly, compared with participants in areas with low levels of both PM 2.5 and CO, the adjusted HR was 1.12 (95% CI: 1.07–1.17) for those in areas with low PM 2.5 but high CO, and 1.28 (95% CI: 1.22–1.33) for those exposed to high levels of both pollutants.

### Sensitivity analyses

Associations stratified by relocation status ( Supplementary Table S2 ) remained significant among participants who stayed in the same township throughout follow-up or during the 3 years prior to their health exam, with slightly stronger effects in the latter group. Stratification by quintile-based township area ( Supplementary Table S3 ) showed that associations were maintained in smaller townships; however, in larger areas (≥62.70 km 2 ), associations for PM 2.5 and NO 2 were attenuated, whereas those for CO remained significant. Robustness analyses considering a high censoring rate (65.7% censored before 2016) confirmed consistency with primary findings ( Supplementary Table S4 ), supporting their validity.

Figure 1 depicts associations of PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO exposure with NAFLD incidence stratified by sex and modifiable behaviors (smoking, sleep, exercise, and fried-food consumption). Participants with unhealthy behaviors were more susceptible to NAFLD when exposed to PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO.
Discussion:
This population-based cohort study highlights significant associations between long-term exposure to PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO, and NAFLD incidence among participants without alcohol consumption.

Several metabolic indicators (abdominal obesity, hypertension, elevated fasting blood glucose, and dyslipidemia) were adjusted for ( Table 3 , Model 3), given the established coexistence of NAFLD with metabolic disorders [ 10 , 11 , 41 ]. Our findings align with Sun et al. , who reported a positive link between PM 2.5 and NAFLD by using the fatty liver index, derived from triglycerides, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, BMI, and waist circumference [ 46 ].

With a mean follow-up of 5.7 years, our findings support the 3-year average as a reliable exposure metric. Supplementary Tables S5 and S6 demonstrate consistent results for various exposure windows (1-, 3-, and 5-year averages) and this finding aligns with prior studies using various exposure windows [ 25 , 28 , 30 ]. Furthermore, our observed NAFLD incidence (53.0 cases per 1000 person-years) closely matches the pooled estimate by Riazi et al. (46.9 cases per 1000 person-years) [ 3 ], confirming the validity of our exposure metric.

As in most follow-up studies, there is a possibility of loss to follow-up. Moreover, participants in the MJ cohort are invited annually for health check-ups, though the actual timing of health examinations varies among individuals. Supplementary Table S7 presents stratified analyses based on follow-up interval length to address potential differences in population characteristics. Results consistently showed significant associations between each pollutant and NAFLD incidence, regardless of the interval length.

Emerging evidence highlights the role of air pollution in NAFLD, with pollutant levels and regional variations influencing risk. In the UK Biobank study, detrimental PM 2.5 ranged from ∼9.7 to 10.9 μg/m³, and NO 2 from 26.4 to 38.7 μg/m³ (∼14.0 to 20.6 ppb, converted at 25°C) [ 29 ]. In contrast, our study identified unique risk patterns from pollutant combinations. Participants living in areas with both high PM 2.5 (>30.2 μg/m³) and NO 2 (>21.6 ppb), low PM 2.5 but high CO (>0.56 ppm), or both high PM 2.5 and CO were at increased risk of NAFLD ( Table 4 ). These differences might be attributable to regional variations in PM 2.5 composition, such as copper and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, linked to hepatic steatosis and lipid metabolism gene expression in experimental studies [ 31 ].

Recently, observational studies have linked NAFLD incidence with residential proximity to major roadways [ 27 ] and NO 2 exposure [ 25 , 29 ], highlighting traffic-related air pollution. This is the first study to longitudinally examine CO exposure and NAFLD incidence. While low CO levels may be cytoprotective, high levels can inhibit cytochrome c oxidase, disrupt mitochondrial metabolism, and induce oxidative stress [ 47 ]. These mechanisms align with our findings.

The strengths of the study include the focus on Taiwan’s densely populated western regions; the evaluation of PM 2.5 , NO 2 , and CO; and the novel association identified between CO exposure and NAFLD. Additionally, culture-specific emission sources, such as temples and Chinese restaurants, were incorporated into the air pollution modeling. More importantly, based on our findings and those of previous studies [ 25 , 30 ], we recommend health promotion strategies to mitigate the effects of air pollution on NAFLD, including reducing fried-food consumption, quitting smoking, ensuring sufficient sleep, and engaging in physical activity. While our study incorporated cultural and behavioral factors, high-resolution models such as 3D GEOS-Chem enable more precise neighborhood-level exposure estimates [ 48 ]. Future research should integrate detailed regional emission inventories to refine exposure assessments and better analyse small-scale sources.

However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, participants potentially had higher socioeconomic status [ 40 ] and greater health consciousness than the general population, which may limit generalizability. Nevertheless, the population density closely resembles Taiwan’s distribution ( Supplementary Figure S2 ), ensuring some degree of representativeness. Second, study participants were selected from the MJ cohort based on abdominal ultrasonography and absence of baseline NAFLD-related conditions, with those missing key covariate data (e.g. lifestyle factors and metabolic indicators) excluded ( Supplementary Table S8 ). Additionally, 65.7% were censored before 2016, raising further concerns regarding representativeness as well. However, the major outcome of this investigation, NAFLD, was obtained by measurement, i.e. abdominal sonography, and not by the capturing of an event, such as cardiac events [ 49 ]. Therefore, the observed outcome might not be related to the censoring. As suggested by Lesko et al. [ 49 ], the follow-up time should be censored at participants' last recorded encounter, reducing concerns of bias due to loss to follow-up, especially in a group of health examinees. This is supported by the AIPW analysis ( Supplementary Table S4 ) , which showed consistent results with the primary findings, supporting the robustness of our study despite substantial attrition. Third, while polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in PM 2.5 are hypothesized to induce hepatic steatosis [ 31 ], our study did not explore this aspect. Instead, we included industrial parks in the air pollution exposure assessment. Future research should examine the long-term effects of specific PM 2.5 components. Fourth, using township-level residential data to estimate personal exposure may have introduced bias due to exposure misclassification, which is inevitable in air pollution studies. This issue relates to the resolution of exposure assessment. High-resolution models, such as 3D GEOS-Chem, have been proposed to provide more precise neighborhood-level exposure estimates [ 48 ]. In this current investigation, township was used as the exposure unit, rather than the exact address. We took into consideration the working and commuting possibilities and opted to use a slightly broader exposure geographic location. Despite this limitation, our exposure model demonstrated reasonably good performance in terms of R 2 and RMSE. To further evaluate the robustness of our findings, we conducted additional analyses (Supplementary Tables S3). Future studies should incorporate higher-resolution exposure data, such as personal air quality monitors or detailed indoor and occupational exposure assessments, to further refine estimates.

In conclusion, long-term exposure to PM 2.5 and traffic-related air pollutants, such as NO 2 and CO, is associated with an increased incidence of NAFLD. These associations, confirmed in two-pollutant models, are particularly relevant for regions with high NAFLD prevalence and air pollution, such as Asia and developing countries.
